Here we introduce SpatialZoomer, a spectral graph-based method that applies a set of low-pass filters to efficiently extract spatial molecular features from spatial transcriptomics data at multiple resolutions or scales, including the single cell scale, the niche scale with dozens of closely interacting cells and the domain scale with spatially organized cell contents. The corresponding critical scales can be automatically identified by partitioning a cross-scale similarity map. Results show that SpatialZoomer can identify disease-progression signals at specific scales in Alzheimer’s disease and spatial context-dependent cell subtypes in tumour microenvironment. The extracted multi-scale features also uncovered spatially heterogeneous niches in cancer. SpatialZoomer achieves comparable or superior performance to existing methods for single-scale tasks, and it also has the advantages of high computational efficiency and low hardware requirements.

title: From pandemic response to a global scientific network via Tissue Talks
abstract: Six years and more than 250 lectures after its launch as a pandemic response, Tissue Talks has reached over 50,000 attendees across more than 80 countries, offering a blueprint for how biomedical communities can maintain continuous global connection beyond the annual conference cycle.

title: Engineering gut microbiome states overcomes hepatic accumulation of nanomedicines
Keeping psychedelics in mind
Towards physiologically relevant human tissue models
abstract: Advances in organoids, organs-on-chips and microphysiological systems are bringing human tissue models closer to the physiological complexity needed to study disease, evaluate therapies and inform precision medicine.

title: Animal numbers are not a proxy for scientific strength
abstract: Judicious animal model design and selection, rather than experimental excess, is key to generating robust, informative and ethically responsible evidence in biomedical research.

title: An interpretable AI model decodes the rules of cell recruitment to specific destinations
abstract: An interpretable neural network, SPACER, learns the rules of cellular recruitment directly from tissue spatial transcriptomics data. Analyses of multiple cancers reveal a role for the local antigen presentation machinery and tumour mucins in T cell recruitment to tumours, and a mouse model of severe checkpoint inhibitor-induced myocarditis identifies CD4+ T cells as key disease effectors.

title: Gradient-driven microfluidic framework for the screening of ratiometric drug combinations towards precision oncology in paediatric leukaemia
abstract: Improving outcomes for high-risk acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) patients requires increasingly personalized treatment strategies that leverage molecular and omics-based assays as well as functional screens. However, to date, only a few of these approaches are clinically actionable and easily adopted in clinical settings. To that end, we report a combination drug screening assay (GradientScreen) that correlates with clinical outcomes using standard paediatric ALL treatment protocols. This assay uses a microfluidic device to generate overlapping drug gradients and implements an analysis framework that characterizes drug synergy and efficacy in a ratiometric manner. Using partial least squares regression, we show that our combination response metrics correlate with both minimal residual disease (MRD) following initiation of treatment and later clinical end-points. Here, we further demonstrate that this system could be used to evaluate response to experimental therapeutic regimens in patients who did not respond to standard treatment. This assay can serve as a research-enabling tool for the field, with potential to integrate into clinical pathology workflows to identify difficult-to-treat ALL patients and screen for alternative treatment strategies at diagnosis.

title: Autologous erythrocyte microparticles drive antitumour T cell immunity via haem-mediated dendritic cell activation
abstract: Current vaccine adjuvants, such as aluminum salts and emulsions, are limited by weak induction of cytotoxic T cell immunity and restricted ability to promote T helper type 1 responses, highlighting the need for safer and more effective alternatives. Here we show that microparticles generated from erythrocytes by controlled ultraviolet irradiation function as potent T helper type 1-skewing adjuvants that enhance tumour antigen-specific cytotoxic T cell responses in vitro and in multiple mouse tumour models. Following uptake by dendritic cells, these microparticles traffic to lysosomes and deliver haem cargo that is subsequently transported to the nucleus. Mechanistically, the particles elevate lysosomal pH, promoting lysosome movement towards the nucleus and enabling haem transfer, where haem activates REV-ERB⍺ and forms a co-repressor complex that suppresses peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma, thereby relieving inhibition of dendritic cell maturation and antigen presentation. In vaccination settings, combining tumour antigens with erythrocyte-derived microparticles enhances cytotoxic T cell activation and suppresses tumour growth with minimal toxicity. These findings establish host-derived vesicles as a promising platform for next-generation cancer vaccine adjuvants.

title: Hydrogel for sustained and localized delivery of a regulatory T cell-inducing agent promotes bone regeneration
abstract: Local activation of regulatory T (T reg ) cells represents a promising strategy for wound repair and tissue regeneration. However, current T reg -based therapies rely on adoptive cell transfer, which requires ex vivo expansion and reinfusion, posing challenges to donor variability and tissue specificity. Here we engineer a hydrogel-based system for in situ T reg activation at injury sites through the controlled release of AS2863619 (AS), a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor. AS is incorporated into collagen hydrogels at concentrations exceeding its solubility limit, reducing burst release and extending the release half-life. This continuous exposure to T reg -inducing agents stabilizes Foxp3 expression in CD4 + T cells, thereby enabling T reg induction and stabilization. The incorporation of laponite nanoparticles further slows AS release and prolongs drug retention. In a calvarial bone-defect model, AS-loaded hydrogels induce dose-dependent T reg cell activation, reduce pro-inflammatory macrophage responses and enhance bone regeneration. Notably, AS–laponite hydrogels achieve complete defect bridging in some cases. By providing spatiotemporal control over T reg populations without the need for cell isolation and expansion, this approach offers a scalable alternative for immunomodulation and tissue repair.

title: Red blood cell-derived extracellular vesicles as a potent autologous adjuvant
abstract: Microparticles released from ultraviolet-irradiated erythrocytes enhance anti-tumoural T cell immunity.

title: Retraction Note: Engineered outer membrane vesicles enhance solid tumour CAR-T cell therapy
abstract: The editors have retracted this article at the authors’ request. After publication, concerns were raised about the data underlying several of the figures. The source data for Figures 5 and 6 as well as Supplementary Figures S10b, S10c, S10f, S10g, S12a, and S14b exhibit unusual numerical patterns where some blocks of observations appear to be mathematically related to other blocks of measurements that should be independent.

title: Cartilage-binding coacervate with therapeutic payload delivery and biomimetic lubrication alleviates osteoarthritis by reducing joint friction and inflammation
abstract: Healthy articular cartilage maintains ultralow friction through the lipid/hyaluronic acid/lubricin complex lubrication layer, in which the zwitterionic lipids mediate lubrication and the hyaluronic acid and lubricin anchor to cartilage matrix. However, in osteoarthritis this lubrication system is progressively degraded, leading to increased cartilage wear and joint dysfunction. Therefore, early and lubrication-based intervention is urgently needed. Here we present biomimetic polyzwitterionic coacervates (pZCOs) that recapitulate both the lubrication and cartilage-binding functionalities of the natural boundary lubrication layer. pZCOs exhibit strong binding affinity to fibronectin, establish a stable and ultralow-friction lubrication layer on the cartilage surface, facilitate the sustained release of anti-inflammatory drugs, and preserve the viability and anti-inflammatory paracrine secretion of encapsulated mesenchymal stem cells. In both rat and mini-pig models of osteoarthritis, intra-articular administration of drug/MSC-laden pZCOs effectively reduces cartilage degradation, suppresses inflammation and promotes cartilage integrity, outperforming clinical hyaluronic acid lubricants in lubrication performance, in vivo retention and therapeutic efficacy. These findings highlight the translational potential of engineered biomimetic coacervates as next-generation joint lubricants for integrated management of osteoarthritis.

title: Author Correction: Advanced glycation end-products as mediators of the aberrant crosslinking of extracellular matrix in scarred liver tissue
Optimal closed-loop feedback control of blood flow after spinal cord injury with norepinephrine
abstract: After spinal cord injury, clinical management aims to support tissue perfusion, but current methods rely on the indirect control of arterial blood pressure without direct measurement of the local blood flow. This limits the ability to tailor drug delivery to the injured tissue. Here, we show that spinal cord blood flow can be regulated using a closed-loop controller that adjusts vasopressor infusion on the basis of real-time ultrasound flow measurement. We characterize the dynamic relationship between drug infusion, arterial pressure and spinal cord blood flow, and we use these data to design a feedback controller that targets a predefined flow level. We validate the system in simulations, implement the controller in real time in rodents and translate it to pigs. We show that the controller reduced blood flow deviations and variability compared with constant dosing and supported functional recovery in a rodent survival model. These results show a closed-loop spinal cord perfusion control strategy that leverages clinically available measurements and pharmacological interventions, supporting its translation to clinical settings for the management of acute spinal cord injury.

title: Closing the loop on blood flow control in spinal cord injury
abstract: After spinal cord injury, clinicians raise blood pressure to protect tissue without directly monitoring the effect on the cord, exposing patients to harm. We designed a closed-loop controller that adjusts drug infusion in response to ultrasonography-based measurements of spinal cord blood flow, stabilizing perfusion at the injury site and preserving neurological function in animals.

title: A single-step injectable Janus-adhesive hydrogel for endoscopic gastrointestinal fistula repair
abstract: Gastrointestinal fistulas (GFs) represent one of the main causes of morbidity and mortality. While endoscopic techniques provide a minimally invasive approach to GF repair, offering advantages over conventional surgical approaches, the integration of endoscopic delivery with hydrogel sealants in user-friendly and easy processes approaches remains a great challenge. Here we develop a thermoresponsive positively charged poly( N -isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM)/Ga 3+ (PGa III ) hydrogel sealant, formed by slug-inspired biomimetic self-assembly. The PGa III integrated injectability and single-step-formed Janus-type adhesion to tissues, simultaneously featuring excellent biocompatibility, water/acid resistance, active shrinkage and antibacterial properties, enabling its effective ready-to-use biological sealant for endoscopic repair of GFs and prevention of postoperative adhesions. To validate the efficacy of PGa III in treating GFs, we demonstrate its effectiveness in repairing GFs and its convenience in non-invasive endoscopic surgery in living Sprague–Dawley rat and Bama miniature pig models. The proposed PGa III holds potential for the repair of fistulas in other organs in vivo, thereby promoting the establishment of safer and more effective clinical treatment options for related diseases.

title: Re-timing mortality risk through individualized modelling of lifespan trajectories
abstract: There is an urgent global need for affordable, large-scale health screening to enhance preventive care in the ageing population. Using low-cost, non-invasive retinal photographs and leveraging large foundation models, we developed a deep learning-based biomarker, Retinal Mortality Equivalent (RetiME), that directly mapped retinal features to individual mortality risk. Trained on a European cohort and externally validated across three independent external cohorts spanning Southeast Asia, Eurasia and North America, RetiME showed robust associations with all-cause and cause-specific mortality and predicted the incidence of a wide range of systemic and ocular diseases. Crucially, beyond static risk estimation, RetiME re-timed mortality risk by reconstructing personalized lifespan trajectories that were associated with observed mortality outcomes (for example, age of death). Clustering of these trajectories revealed distinct mortality patterns, spanning cancer-predominant, cardiometabolic and neurodegenerative risks, reflecting diverse ageing pathways captured by RetiME. Interpretability analyses showed that RetiME captures diverse biological and retinal features underlying mortality risk. Genome-wide analyses further identified genetic loci associated with RetiME. Collectively, these findings support further evaluation of retinal imaging and trajectory modelling as one component of a comprehensive assessment of mortality risk.

title: Author Correction: Intravascularly infused extracellular matrix as a biomaterial for targeting and treating inflamed tissues
Non-invasive oral magnetoelectric vagus nerve neuromodulation for Parkinson’s disease therapy
abstract: Vagus nerve stimulation has shown promising neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in progressive neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson’s disease. However, its invasive nature introduces procedural and device-related risks. Here we introduce a magnetoelectric particulate system for oral delivery and non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation through the gut. The system comprises a magneto-responsive nickel ferrite core and a piezoelectric barium titanate shell, conjugated with capsaicin to specifically target TRPV1 receptors, ensuring effective adherence to the stomach lining after oral administration. Upon magnetic field stimulation, the particles generate electrical pulses that activate vagal afferent fibres, engaging the nucleus tractus solitarius in the brainstem via the gut−brain axis. This activation enhances norepinephrine production in the locus coeruleus and dopamine synthesis in the substantia nigra. Vagal efferent activation triggers the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway, mitigating both neuroinflammation and systemic inflammation. This non-invasive approach demonstrates potential for alleviating motor symptoms and non-motor anxiety in Parkinson’s disease, offering valuable insights into its mechanisms and clinical applications.
